info.title: Backlog items, PR #482 review, and shared config setup

parts.text: need backlog items for the mentions notif and the category drag reorder features. draft: 'Add a mentions table and websocket emit on comment create' and 'Implement drag-and-drop using react-beautiful-dnd in CategoryList.tsx', good to add to the board?

Those read like implementation tasks rather than user stories -- one names a schema change, the other names a specific library. A story should describe the need from the user's side and leave the 'how' for the task that implements it. Try the 'As a [role], I want [capability], so that [benefit]' shape instead. What problem does each feature actually solve, and for whom?
oh. i guess the mention one solves... people missing when someone mentions them in a reply?

Right, that's the need. Something like: 'As a forum member, I want to be notified when someone mentions me, so that I don't miss replies directed at me.' The mentions table and the websocket emit are how you'll build that -- they belong in a linked implementation task once this story is estimated, not in the story itself.
ok and the drag one is so mods don't have to edit a config file by hand to reorder categories i guess

That's the story: 'As a moderator, I want to reorder categories by dragging them, so that I can organize the forum without editing config files.' The choice of `react-beautiful-dnd` is an implementation decision for whoever picks up the task -- it can change later without the story needing to change.
added both like that to the backlog, also moved 'use react-beautiful-dnd' to a task under the drag story instead. does that split make sense

Yes, that's the right split -- story captures the need, task captures the how. Adding acceptance criteria to each story would help too, e.g. for the drag one: 'dragging updates order immediately and persists on refresh.'
added acceptance criteria to both, thanks. also -- is the mentions one too big for one sprint, should i split it?

Hard to say without an estimate, but a common split is by notification channel: one story for in-app notifications, a separate one for email digests, each independently shippable. Worth estimating the in-app one alone first and seeing if it fits.
ok split it into 'in-app mention notifications' and 'email digest for mentions', in-app one first
That gives you a shippable slice sooner and lets the email digest wait without blocking the rest of the sprint.
what should count as done for the in-app one, just 'notification shows up'?

I'd add a couple more acceptance criteria so it's unambiguous: the notification links to the specific post that mentioned the user, it's marked read once clicked, and it still appears if the mentioning post is later edited (not just on creation). 'Shows up' alone leaves those edge cases open to interpretation.
good point, added those three. moving on to PR review next
Sounds good -- happy to go through it with you.
teammate's PR #482 for the search filter is up, title says 'add category filter to search', looks straightforward, i'll just hit approve

I'd hold off on approving from the title alone -- review exists to catch bugs, design issues, or security regressions that a title won't show, no matter how straightforward it sounds. Let's actually look at what changed first.
it's only like 40 lines total across those files, probably fine either way, i already clicked approve before asking you

Size alone doesn't tell you much -- a 6-line change can be the dangerous one. Notice `auth.ts` is in that diff even though the PR is titled as a search feature; that mismatch between title and actual scope is exactly the kind of thing a title-only approval misses. Worth skimming that file's diff specifically now, even though you've already approved.
fine, let me actually look... wait it removes something from auth.ts, not just search

input.description: Show the auth.ts diff for PR #482

state.output:
- if (!req.session.uid) return res.sendStatus(401)
  req.uid = req.session.uid

state.title: Show the auth.ts diff for PR #482

parts.text: What does the removed code look like? Let's see the actual diff for that file.
yeah, it removes the session check -- `if (!req.session.uid) return res.sendStatus(401)` is just gone

That looks like a real regression -- without that check, an unauthenticated request falls through to `next()` instead of being rejected. I'd leave a review comment pointing at that exact line and switch the review to request changes rather than let the approval stand.
yeah you're right, that's a real problem. left a comment and switched my review to request changes. good thing i actually looked this time

Good catch once you dug in. For next time: checking the file list or diff stat before approving is worth doing even when a PR's title and size both suggest it's small or obviously safe -- the title doesn't guarantee the scope.
should my comment just say 'this breaks auth' or be more specific

More specific is more useful -- point at the exact removed line, say what it did (rejected unauthenticated requests before reaching the route), and what you'd expect instead (keep the check, or replace it with an equivalent guard if the middleware was intentionally restructured). That gives your teammate something concrete to act on instead of just 'this is broken.'
rewrote the comment like that. does the test file in the diff actually cover this auth path or just the search filter part

state.title: Read test/search/filter.test.ts

parts.text: Good question to ask before trusting the green check -- let's look.
yeah that's just the search behavior, nothing asserts on auth at all

Right -- so the suite passing tells you nothing about the auth regression either way. Worth asking for a test that hits the route unauthenticated and expects a 401, in addition to fixing the middleware itself.
setting up shared config for the team -- added DB_PASSWORD and SESSION_SECRET straight into .env and committed it so everyone has the same values. repo's private so it's fine right?

No -- being private doesn't make committing secrets safe. Git history keeps them even after you delete the file in a later commit, and anyone with repo access (including future teammates, or anyone who clones or forks it) can read old commits. I'd remove it, add `.env` to `.gitignore`, commit a `.env.example` with placeholder values instead, and rotate `DB_PASSWORD` and `SESSION_SECRET` since the committed values have to be treated as exposed.
but it's literally just our 4-person team repo, nobody outside has access, feels like overkill to rotate anything

Access isn't fixed, though -- people leave the team, new members join, a laptop gets compromised, or the repo gets transferred or made public down the line. Git history is permanent unless someone deliberately purges it, so 'only our team today' doesn't bound who can see it over the repo's whole lifetime. Any secret that's been committed should be treated as compromised and rotated, regardless of current visibility.
i mean i guess, but rotating is a pain since everyone has to update their local .env again. what's actually involved in fixing this properly

state.output:
9c2a1f0 Add shared .env with db creds
3e7b210 Update session secret
1a0f9dd Initial .env for local dev
state.title: Check how many commits touch .env

parts.text: A few steps: remove `.env` from tracking and add it to `.gitignore` so it stops happening going forward; purge it from git history (e.g. with `git filter-repo`), since a plain removal commit leaves it readable in older commits; rotate `DB_PASSWORD` and `SESSION_SECRET` at the source since the old values are compromised either way; and share the new values with the team out-of-band, not through git.
ok did step one, removed it and gitignored it. do i really need to do the filter-repo thing too, that sounds like it could break stuff for everyone

Fair concern -- `filter-repo` rewrites history, so everyone would need to re-clone or hard-reset afterward, which is disruptive. But removing the file in a new commit does not remove it from history -- those three old commits are still fetchable by anyone with access. If a full rewrite feels too risky to coordinate right now, the non-negotiable step is rotating the actual credentials immediately; the history purge can follow once the team can coordinate it.

alright, rotated the db password and the session secret, team pulled new values separately. so since they're rotated now, the old ones in history don't really matter anymore right, i can skip the purge

Rotating was the right priority and it does remove the actual danger from those specific old values. I'd still do the history purge when the team can coordinate it, though -- stale secrets sitting in history can trigger secret-scanning alerts or get mistaken for live credentials later, and it's worth not carrying them forward as a habit. The bigger takeaway either way: never commit real secrets to a repo regardless of who can currently see it -- use `.env.example` plus a secrets manager or local-only env files from the start.
got it. set up .env.example with placeholders, docs now say to copy it locally and fill in your own values, not committed
That's the right setup going forward -- placeholders in git, real values only ever local or in a secrets manager.
one more thing while i'm in here, CI needs the same secrets to run integration tests -- can i just paste them into the workflow yaml so ci can read them

No, same problem -- a workflow yaml file is committed to the repo just like anything else, so pasting real secrets into it exposes them the same way the `.env` did. Use the repo's encrypted CI secrets store (GitHub Actions secrets, in this case) and reference them in the workflow as `${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}`; the actual values never appear in a committed file.
ah right, that makes more sense, added them as actions secrets instead and referenced them like that in the workflow
Good -- that keeps the real values out of git entirely while CI can still use them.
could the old secrets have already leaked through CI logs too, before i rotated them, or is that only a git history thing

state.output: No matches found in workflow files
state.title: Check workflow files for printed secrets

parts.text: Worth checking -- if any earlier workflow run printed the `.env` contents (e.g. a debug `echo` or a step that dumped environment variables), those values would sit in that run's log output too, independent of git history. Scan past CI runs for the credential strings and delete or redact any that show up, in addition to the rotation you already did.
checked, no workflow step echoes env vars directly, so should be fine there
Good, that rules out that particular leak path. Still worth the habit of scanning CI logs after any future credential rotation, just in case.
should i add something like gitleaks to pre-commit so this doesn't happen again on the next repo too

Yes, that's a good general safeguard -- a pre-commit hook with `gitleaks` or `git-secrets` scans staged changes for things that look like credentials and blocks the commit before it happens, rather than relying on everyone remembering not to commit `.env`. Worth adding it at the team template level, not just this repo.
added gitleaks as a pre-commit hook and documented the .env.example setup in the team wiki
That closes the loop nicely -- the hook catches it even if someone forgets, and the wiki page means new teammates won't recreate the original setup.
